opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's one of the things that surprised us most, honestly. The core idea is the latent action model. We train it on video alone, without any action labels. The model sees a sequence of past frames plus the next frame, and it has to infer some latent action that explains the transition. Then a decoder has to reconstruct that next frame using only the past frames and that latent action.

The trick is the bottleneck. We quantize the latent action into a very small discrete codebook, around eight actions. Because the decoder already has the history, the latent doesn't need to encode everything about the next frame. It only needs to encode what you can't predict from the past, and with so few codes it can't just memorize pixels. So what's left tends to be the part of the change that's controllable, like the character moving left, moving right, or jumping.

As for why it stays consistent across environments, that comes from sharing one codebook across the whole dataset. We trained on a huge amount of 2D platformer footage, and those games share a lot of structure. There's usually a main character, and the ways it can move are roughly the same everywhere. The cheapest way for the model to use eight codes across thousands of different games is to reuse the same code for the same kind of motion. So "action three" ends up meaning something like "jump," whether the game is pixel art or a kid's sketch.

We didn't explicitly supervise any of that. It came out of the compression pressure plus the diversity of the data. And that's what makes it exciting to me. You can hand the model an image it's never seen, even a photo or a drawing, press the same latent action, and get a sensible, consistent behavior. It isn't perfect. Sometimes the codes are a bit entangled, or the model picks the wrong thing as the controllable agent. But the fact that a meaningful, transferable action space falls out of unlabeled internet video felt like a real step toward learning world models at scale.

r001.rationale: The response says the action space was not explicitly supervised and emerged from compression pressure and diverse video data.

r002.rationale: It describes learning latent actions to reconstruct the next frame, then explains that a shared codebook across environments encourages reusing codes for the same kinds of motion.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is honestly one of the things that surprised us the most when we were building Genie. We never explicitly told the model what an action was. There are no action labels anywhere in the training data. It's just hundreds of thousands of hours of internet video of people playing platformer games, and all we have is the sequence of frames.

So the way we set it up is with what we call a latent action model. It looks at a frame and the next frame and tries to infer a discrete latent code that explains the transition between them. And the key design choice is that we make that bottleneck really small. We use a VQ-VAE style codebook, and in the paper we only have eight codes. So the model is forced to compress whatever changed between those two frames into one of eight possible things.

And what happens is, because that bottleneck is so tight, the model can't afford to waste codes on things that are specific to a single game. It has to find the most reusable explanation for change across the whole dataset. And it turns out the most reusable explanation is essentially the agent's control. Like, "the character moved left," "the character moved right," "the character jumped." Those are the things that are consistent across almost every 2D platformer, even though the sprites, the backgrounds, the physics all look completely different.

There's also a nice inductive bias from the decoder side. The dynamics model gets the past frames plus the latent action and has to predict the next frame. So the latent action is really only useful to the extent that it carries information the frames themselves don't already have. The background scrolling, the enemies moving around, those are mostly predictable from context. The thing that isn't predictable is what the player decided to do. So the latent code naturally gets pushed toward capturing agent intent rather than environmental stuff.

Now, I want to be careful here. We don't have a guarantee that code three means "jump" in every environment. What we observed empirically is that the actions were remarkably consistent. You could take the same latent action and apply it in a generated world from a sketch, or a real photo, or a totally unseen game, and you'd get semantically similar behavior. We found that pretty striking. But there is some variability, and some codes are a bit more like "no-op" or "something ambiguous happened."

The other thing I'd add is that scale really mattered here. At smaller scales, the latent actions were much noisier and more entangled with visual changes. As we scaled the model and the data, they got cleaner and more controllable. So I think part of the answer is just that with enough diverse data, the controllable factor is the thing that generalizes, and the model learns to isolate it because that's what minimizes its loss across everything it's seen.

r001.rationale: The response says the model receives no action labels and infers latent codes from frame transitions, so the mapping emerges without explicit action grounding.

r002.rationale: It explains that predicting the next frame makes the latent action useful for capturing agent intent, while the small bottleneck favors reusable explanations across the dataset’s different games and environments.

astra-6.text:
The way I think about it is that Genie has to discover actions through their effects. It sees video frames, but it doesn’t get labels saying, “This is left,” or “This is jump.” It learns a latent action that helps explain the transition from one frame to the next, and then a dynamics model learns to predict what happens given that action.

Because those models are shared across the training data, there’s an opportunity to reuse the same action representation across different visual environments. Moving left might look different depending on the character and the background, but the underlying change can be similar.

What’s interesting is that consistency emerges without explicitly assigning those meanings to the action codes. But I’d distinguish that from a guarantee that every code has exactly the same meaning in every environment. It’s a learned regularity, and the arbitrary code itself only gets meaning through the effect it produces.

r001.rationale: The response says action meanings are not explicitly assigned and that consistency emerges without explicit meanings for the action codes.

r002.rationale: It links latent actions to explaining frame transitions and predicting what happens, then says the models are shared across training data, creating an opportunity to reuse the same action representation across environments.

sol-6.1.text:
The intuition is that Genie learns actions through their effect on the world. During training, the latent action model looks at consecutive video frames and learns a compact code for the transition between them. The dynamics model then uses that code, along with the previous frames, to predict what happens next.

Because those models are shared across the training data, there’s pressure to reuse codes for similar kinds of changes. So a code that corresponds to moving right can have a similar effect across environments, even when the character or background looks different. Nobody explicitly labels that code “right”; that meaning emerges from learning to predict the transitions.

I’d distinguish that useful consistency from a guarantee that every action has exactly the same meaning in every environment. It’s a learned regularity, rather than something we explicitly enforce with action labels.

r001.rationale: The response says action codes are not explicitly labeled and their meaning emerges from learning to predict transitions.

r002.rationale: It explains that shared models trained across environments create pressure to reuse codes for similar changes, while the dynamics model predicts what happens next.
